## 1 Introduction

All-Pairs Shortest Paths (APSP), which asks given an _N_-vertex graph to compute the distance \(\delta(u,v)\) between all pairs of vertices, is one of the central problems in fine-grained complexity. Classical algorithms for APSP, such as the Floyd-Warshall algorithm, achieve a _O(N_<sup>3</sup>) running time. A long series of works (e.g. \[Fre76, Dob90, Tak92, Tak98, Han04, Pet04, Zwi04, Cha05, Han06, Cha10, HT12\]) improved sub- polynomial factors over the classic _O(N_<sup>3</sup>) running time, culminating in an algorithm by Williams \[Wil18\] with \(N^3/2^{\Theta(\sqrt{logN})}\) running time. Very recently, a major breakthrough by Anthropic (see Alman and Vassilevska Williams \[AV26\]) gave the first truly subcubic algorithm for APSP, falsifying one of the central hypotheses in Fine-Grained Complexity, obtaining a deterministic algorithm in _O(N_<sup>2.9995</sup>) time (see also the simplified exposition due to Karingula and Lovett \[KL26\] that achieves \(O(N^{3-\delta})\) for some \(\delta>0\)). \[AV26\] also obtain a Las Vegas algorithm running in expected time _O(N_<sup>2.998</sup>) for real-valued APSP. In light of this breakthrough, one might naturally expect further improvements to the APSP exponent.

In this note, we give a simple improvement to the exponent of APSP, via a faster algorithm for computing the (min,+) Product of two \(N\times N\) matrices. The (min,+) product of two matrices _A,B_, defined (_A∗B_)\[_i,j_\]=min_<sub>k</sub>A_\[_i,k_\]+_B_\[_k,j_\], is a useful primitive in algorithm design, and is known to be equivalent to APSP up to polylogarithmic factors \[VW18\]. Our first result is an improved randomized algorithm.

**Theorem 1.1.** _There is a Las Vegas algorithm computing the_ (min,+)_-product of two_ \(N\times N\) _matrices A,B with polynomially bounded integer entries in expected time_ \(\tilde{O}\left(N^{2.9963432}\right)\).

Using known reductions, this also gives faster algorithms for many problems equivalent to (min,+)- Matrix Multiplication, including APSP, Negative Triangle, Replacement Paths, Second Shortest Simple Path, Metricity, (min,+)-Verification \[VW18\], Weighted Tree Edit Distance \[BGMW20, NPS<sup>+</sup>25\], and 2D Maximum Subarray \[TT00, BDT16\].

Our algorithm uses a modular approach to tackle the (min,+) product in subcubic time, first proposed by Bringmann, Grandoni, Saha, and Vassilevska Williams \[BGSV19\], and subsequently refined and modified in \[GPVX21, CDXZ22, JPSX26\]. In \[BGSV19\], the very first step of the algorithm is to provide an additive approximation of _C_ by recursively scaling and rounding. This additive approximation is used to perturb the entries of _A_ and _B_ so that many entries of _A_ and _B_ become small. This enables computation of fast (min,+) product over those small entries via fast matrix multiplication \[AGM97\]. Surprisingly, as \[BGSV19\] shows after the perturbation, only a subcubic number of witnesses, triples which can contribute to _C_, are left: this provided a promising route towards refuting the APSP conjecture.

In order to complete this framework and obtain truly subcubic APSP, one needs a sparse certificate to find those remaining triplets. The works of \[BGSV19, GPVX21, CDXZ22, JPSX26\] show such sparse certificate exists for various structured matrices such as bounded difference and monotone matrices. Subsequent work \[GPVX21, CDXZ22, JPSX26\] combine the perturbation and sparse certification steps through modular arithmetic over primes.

We develop on the modular approach of \[BGSV19, GPVX21, CDXZ22, JPSX26\] and utilize Theorem 25 of the recent breakthrough \[AV26\] to provide a sparse certificate in truly subcubic time without any structural assumptions. This leads to a slightly better running time, and a significantly simpler, easy to understand algorithm. We state Theorem 25 of \[AV26\] below.

**Theorem 1.2** (Theorem 25 of \[AV26\])**.** _For every_ \(\varepsilon<\varepsilon^*:=(ln4)/(5ln10)=0.1204\dots\) _and every_ \(\kappa>0\) _there is a_ \(\gamma>0\) _such that the following holds. Given as input matrices_ \(X\in\mathbb{Z}^{N\times D}\) _and_ \(Y\in\mathbb{Z}^{D\times N}\)_, where_ \(2\le D\le N^\varepsilon\)_, whose entries are integers of absolute value at most N_<sup>_O_(1)</sup>_, as well as a set W of at most_ \(N^2/D^\kappa\) _positions of an_ \(N\times N\) _matrix, the entries_ \((XY)[I,J]\), \((I,J)\in W\)_, can be computed deterministically in time_ \(O(N^2log^2D/D^\gamma)\).

To invoke Theorem 1.2, we divide the matrices _A_ and _B_ into blocks and for each block, design a family of new matrices _X_ and _Y_ satisfying the properties of Theorem 1.2 such that computing relevant entries of (_XY_) helps us certify whether a given block of _A_ and _B_ is a candidate in which we ought to look for a witness. We stop whenever the first witness is obtained. Our second result shows that the same exponent can be achieved deterministically.

**Theorem 1.3.** _There is a deterministic algorithm computing the_ (min,+)_-product of two_ \(N\times N\) _matrices A,B with polynomially bounded integer entries in time_ \(\tilde{O}\left(N^{2.9963432}\right)\).

For the sake of simplicity, we present our randomized algorithm in its entirety, and then present the deterministic algorithm separately. We leave as an interesting future direction to further improve the exponent of (min,+) Matrix Multiplication, e.g. by improving the running time of thin matrix product, or to extend our improvements to real-valued matrices.

### Ongoing Work.

The main goal of this note was to give a simplified, modular approach to (min,+) Matrix Multiplication and APSP, and to contextualize the new breakthrough through existing frameworks, thereby facilitating a better intuitive understanding. Any improvement in exponents is a byproduct of that. After prompting ChatGPT with our algorithm, it has suggested further improvements of the running time, as well as extending exponent improvements to real-valued matrices using known reductions \[CVX22\], Lemma 37 of \[AV26\] and re-optimizing the parameters. We are trying to understand if these improvements fit within our simple framework.

### Statement on AI Usage.

For the randomized algorithm, we used publicly available ChatGPT Pro for verification of our approach, optimization of parameters and for numerical calculations. The subsequent ideas for the deterministic algorithm are due to ChatGPT Pro with mild supervision. We have evaluated all proposed arguments, and refined the proof and exposition of the claimed results. The paper was written by the authors, and we take full responsibility for the final manuscript.

## 2 Preliminaries

Let \[_U_\]={1_,...,U_}. log is base 2 and ln is base _e_ unless otherwise specified. For \(p\in[0,1]\), we use _H(p_)=-_p_ln_p_-(1-_p_)ln(1-_p_) to denote entropy. For a matrix _A_, let _A_\[_i,k_\] denote the (_i,k_)-th entry of _A_. For matrices _A,B_, let _AB_ denote the standard matrix product and _A∗B_ denote the (min,+) product. Let T<sub>MUL</sub>(_N_<sub>1</sub>_,N_<sub>2</sub>_,N_<sub>3</sub>) denote the time required to compute the product of a \(N_1\times N_2\) matrix and \(N_2\times N_3\) matrix. We use \(\omega\) to denote the matrix multiplication exponent, i.e. the infimum over all constants such that two \(N\times N\) matrices can be multiplied in \(N^{\omega+o(1)}\) time. It is known \(\omega\le 9/4\) \[Ope26\], although for our purposes, weaker bounds on \(\omega\) will suffice. Our algorithm makes use of the prime number theorem.

**Theorem 2.1** (Prime Number Theorem)**.** _Let_ \(\pi(x)\) _denote the number of primes at most x. The prime number theorem states that_<tbc>

\(\pi(x)=\frac{x}{lnx}(1+o(1)).\)

<tbc>_As a corollary, for any sufficiently large integer R, the number of primes in the interval_ \[_R,_2_R_\] _is_

\(\pi(2R)-\pi(R)=\Theta(R/logR).\)

## 3 Faster \(\left(min,+\right)\) Matrix Multiplication

We present the proof of Theorem 1.1.

_Proof of Theorem 1.1._ By a standard reduction (e.g. shifting all entries by a large constant), we may assume that every input value is a positive integer. We follow the framework of previous algorithms for Bounded Difference and Monotone (min,+) Matrix Multiplication.

### Step 1: Reduction to Verification via Additive Approximation.

First, by a standard reduction (see e.g. Section 4.1 of \[JPSX26\]), we observe that it suffices to reduce to the following witness finding problem.

**Definition 3.1.** _Given_ \(A,B,C\in\mathbb{Z}^{N\times N}\)_, the_ (min,+)_-Witness Equality problem asks to check for all i,j, whether there exists_ \(k\in[N]\) _such that A_\[_i,k_\]+_B_\[_k,j_\]=_C_\[_i,j_\].

**Lemma 3.2** (Tight Reduction to Verification)**.** _Suppose_ (min,+)_-Witness Equality can be computed in time T(N,U_) _whenever A,B have entries in_ \[_U_\] _and C has entries in_ \[2_U_\]_. Then the_ (min,+)_-Product of two_ \(N\times N\) _integer matrices with entries in_ \[_U_\] _can be computed in time_

\(O\left((T(N,U)+N^2)logU\right).\)

We defer the proof of Lemma 3.2 and focus on providing an algorithm for (min,+)-Witness Equality. The idea is essentially that from \(\lceil A/2\rceil*\lceil B/2\rceil\), we can obtain a +2-approximation of _A∗B_. Then, invoking the oracle for (min,+)-Witness Equality _O_(1) times, we can check all 3 possible values of (_A∗B_)\[_i,j_\] for each _i,j_. We say (_i,j_) is accurate if there exists \(k\in[N]\) such that _A_\[_i,k_\]+_B_\[_k,j_\]=_C_\[_i,j_\]. By Lemma 3.2, it suffices to check for whether every pair (_i,j_) is accurate.

### Step 2: Finding a Sparse Certificate.

In this step, our goal is to efficiently prune triples (_i,k,j_) for which \(A[i,k]+B[k,j]\neq C[i,j]\). Fix parameters \(1\le B,S\le N\) whose values we will determine later and let \(P\gg BlogU\) for some sufficiently large constant. Split the inner dimension \[_N_\] into _O(N/B_) contiguous blocks of size _B_. A block _K_ is a _block witness_ for output pair (_i,j_) if there exists \(k\in K\) such that _A_\[_i,k_\]+_B_\[_k,j_\]=_C_\[_i,j_\]. Since _K_ are disjoint and cover \[_N_\], observe that (_i,j_) is accurate if and only if there is a block witness _K_.

To find block witnesses efficiently, we begin by finding a set of candidate witnesses. Let \(p\in[P,2P]\) be a prime. For a block _K_ and prime _p_, we say _K_ is a _candidate block witness_ with respect to _p_ for (_i,j_) if there exists \(k\in K\) satisfying

\(A[i,k]+B[k,j]\equiv C[i,j]modp.\)

We have the following claim.

**Claim 3.3** (Candidate Block Witness)**.** _Fix_ \(i,j\in[N]\)_. If K is a block witness, then K is a candidate block witness with respect to p for any choice of prime p._

_Let p_∼\[_P,_2_P_\] _be a randomly sampled prime. If K is not a block witness, then K is not a candidate block witness with respect to p with probability_ \(\ge 1/2\) _over the choice of p._

_Proof of Claim 3.3._ The first claim is trivial, so we focus on the second. Since _K_ is not a block witness, for \(k\in[K]\) define<tbc>

\(\Delta_k:=A[i,k]+B[k,j]-C[i,j]\neq 0.\)

<tbc>Note that \(0<|\Delta_k|\le 3U\) so that \(\Delta_k\) has at most \(O(log_PU)=O\left(\frac{logU}{logP}\right)\) prime factor in the range \[_P,_2_P_\]. By the prime number theorem, there are \(\Theta(P/logP)\) primes in the range \[_P,_2_P_\] so that for a random choice of prime _p_∼\[_P,_2_P_\], the probability that \(\Delta_k\equiv 0modp\) is at most

\(O\left(\frac{logU}{logP}\frac{logP}{P}\right)=O\left(\frac{logU}{P}\right).\)

A union bound ensures that \(\Delta_k\equiv 0modp\) for any \(k\in K\) with probability at most _O(B_log_U/P_). By our choice of \(P\gg BlogU\), the probability can be upper bounded by 1/2.

This motivates the following approach: sample _O_(log_n_) primes independently in the range \[_P,_2_P_\]. We say _K_ is a _candidate block witness_ if _K_ is a candidate block witness with respect to all sampled primes _p_. Any block that is a block witness will be a candidate block witness, whereas any block that is not a block witness will be a candidate block witness with inverse polynomial probability. Our first goal is to generate candidate block witnesses algorithmically. To do so, we give a subroutine that given block _K_ and prime _p_, checks whether _K_ is a candidate block witness with respect to _p_.

**Lemma 3.4** (Candidate Block Witness Verification)**.** _Let K be a block and_ \(p\in[P,2P]\) _be a prime. For every_ \(\varepsilon<\varepsilon^*:=(\mathrm{ln}4)/(5\mathrm{ln}10)=0.1204\dots\) _and every_ \(\kappa>0\) _there is a_ \(\gamma>0\) _such that the following holds._

_If_ \(2BP\le N^\varepsilon\)_, there is an algorithm that decides for every pair_ (_i,j_) _whether K is a candidate block witness with respect to p for_ (_i,j_) _in time_

\(\tilde{O}\left(N^2+NBP^2+N^2P^{1-\gamma} B^{-\gamma}+(BP)^{\kappa-\gamma} N^2\right).\)

## Step 3: Verifying the Sparse Certificate

Given Lemma 3.4, we present our algorithm for (min,+)- Witness Equality. In this final step, we search all candidate block witnesses and check if they are true block witnesses. As discussed, we begin by sampling random primes and generating all candidate block witnesses for every pair (_i,j_).

Correctness of the above procedure follows by the correctness of Lemma 3.4 and the definition of candidate block witnesses. The time required over all _O(N/B_) blocks _K_ and _O_(log_S_) primes _p_ is

\(\tilde{O}\left(\frac{N^3}{B}+N^2P^2+\frac{N^3P^{1-\gamma}}{B^{1+\gamma}}+\frac{N^3(BP)^{\kappa-\gamma}}{B}\right).\)

For a pair (_i,j_), let _K(i,j_) denote the set of candidate block witnesses. In the second phase, we test whether a candidate block witness is a block witness. We use the following algorithm for every pair (_i,j_).

Correctness of the algorithm follows from the fact that Claim 3.3 implies that every block witness is a candidate block witness. Thus, if (_i,j_) is accurate, we will eventually iterate over a block witness in _K(i,j_) and enumerate the witness _k_ such that _A_\[_i,k_\]+_B_\[_k,j_\]=_C_\[_i,j_\]. On the other hand, if (_i,j_) is not accurate, no check will succeed.

To bound the running time, we separately bound the time required to process block witnesses and false candidates (i.e. candidate block witnesses that are not block witnesses). Since we terminate after any successful check, we process at most 1 block witness for every pair (_i,j_), resulting in total time _O(N_<sup>2</sup>_B_) to process all block witnesses. To bound the time required to process false candidates, we bound the total number of false candidates. From Claim 3.3, a block _K_ that is not a block witness is a candidate block witness with probability at most \(2^{-\lceil logS\rceil}\le S^{-1}\). Since there are _N_<sup>2</sup> (_i,j_) pairs and _O(N/B_) blocks per pair, the total number of false candidates is in expectation at most _O(N_<sup>3</sup>/(_BS_)), resulting in _O(N_<sup>3</sup>_/S_) expected time to process all false candidates. Overall, the expected runtime of our algorithm is

\(\tilde{O}\left(\frac{N^3}{B}+N^2P^2+\frac{N^3P^{1-\gamma}}{B^{1+\gamma}}+\frac{N^3(BP)^{\kappa-\gamma}}{B}+N^2B+N^3/S\right).\)

Recall that we require \(P\gg BlogU\), so that minimizing _P_ subject to this constraint, the running time is

\(\tilde{O}\left(\frac{N^3}{B}+N^2B^2log^2U+N^3B^{-2\gamma} logU+N^3B^{2\kappa-2\gamma-1}logU+N^2B+N^3/S\right).\)

Setting _S=N_ and simplifying (e.g. recalling \(\kappa\ge\gamma\)), we obtain the running time

\(\tilde{O}\left(\frac{N^3B^{2(\kappa-\gamma)}}{B}logU+N^2B^2log^2U+N^3B^{-2\gamma} logU\right).\)

We prove the remaining required reduction to (min,+)-Witness Equality for completeness. The proof is essentially identical to \[JPSX26\], with the only change being that the input and output matrices are not required to be monotone.

_Proof of Lemma 3.2._ We recurse on the value of _U_. In the base case where _U_=1, return (_A∗B_)\[_i,j_\]=2 for all (_i,j_).

Then, suppose _U\>_1. Without loss of generality, suppose _U_ is a power of 2. We begin by constructing matrices \(A',B'\) as follows<tbc>

\(A'=\lceil A/2\rceil,B'=\lceil B/2\rceil\)

<tbc>and recursively compute \(X'=A'*B'\). It is easy to see that \(A',B'\) have values in \[_U/_2\].

Let _X=A⋆B_. For every triple _i,k,j_, observe that<tbc>

\(2(A'[i,k]+B'[k,j]-1)\le A[i,k]+B[k,j]\le 2(A'[i,k]+B'[k,j]).\)

<tbc>Taking minima over _k_ yields

\(2X'[i,j]-2\le X[i,j]\le 2X'[i,j]\)

for every pair (_i,j_). Thus, \(X[i,j]\in\{2X'[i,j]-2,2X'[i,j]-1,2X'[i,j]\}\).

For each \(s\in\{-2,-1,0\}\) run the (min,+)-Witness Equality algorithm with candidate matrix \(C_s[i,j]=2X'[i,j]+s\in[2U]\) since \(2\le X'[i,j]\le U\). For every (_i,j_), return the smallest \(2X'[i,j]+s\) for which the (min,+)-Witness Equality algorithm reports that there exists _k_ such that

\(A[i,k]+B[k,j]=2X'[i,j]+s.\)

Note that this algorithm is correct since \(X[i,j]\in\{2X'[i,j]-2,2X'[i,j]-1,2X'[i,j]\}\), so that the minimum value with a witness must be the true value of the (min,+) product.

Let _M(N,U_) denote the time required to compute the product of two \(N\times N\) matrices with entries in \[_U_\]. By the master theorem, the total time required is

\(M(N,U)=M(N,U/2)+O\left((T(N,U)+N^2)\right)=O\left((T(N,U)+N^2)logU\right).\)

## 3.1 Derandomization

Next, we discuss how to derandomize Theorem 1.1.

_Proof of Theorem 1.3._ Observe that in the proof of Theorem 1.1 the only randomization required is to sample primes in Step 2, finding a sparse certificate. Thus, we may choose \(P=\Theta(BlogU)\) to bound this probability by a constant, say 1/2. In fact, by independently selecting _s_ random primes \(p\in\mathcal{P}\), one can reduce this probability to 2<sup>-_s_</sup>. To derandomize the above approach, we will instead show how to deterministically find primes \(p\in\mathcal{P}\) that reduce the number of false candidates.

At level \(\ell\), we will ensure that the number of false candidates is upper bounded by a function \(\Phi^{(\ell)}:=\Theta\left(\frac{N^3}{B2^{7\ell}}\right)\), a bound which is trivially satisfied at \(\ell=0\). We will deterministically choose a constant number of primes such that the number of false level \(\ell\) candidates decreases by a factor of 2<sup>7</sup>. We know that a random prime will eliminate all but a \(O\left(\frac{B^{(\ell)}logU}{P}\right)=O(2^{-\ell})\) fraction of false candidates. Thus, a natural attempt is to deterministically choose a prime _p_ that eliminates the largest fraction of false candidates (or minimize \(\Phi^{(\ell)}\)). Unfortunately, both the quantity of false candidates eliminated by a given prime _p_ (and \(\Phi^{(\ell)}\)) may be hard to compute, as it may involve checking whether a candidate is genuine or not (see \[JPSX26\] for further discussion). Instead, we find a function _Z(p_) that is a constant-factor approximation of \(\Phi^{(\ell)}\) (Lemma 3.8) and we can efficiently compute (Lemma 3.9). This indirect approach of finding an estimate of the desired bound that is easier to compute is similar to \[JPSX26\], although our estimator is distinct and tailored to our specific application. Thus, choosing a prime _p_ that minimizes _Z(p_) suffices to ensure that the number of false candidates decreases by a factor of \(O(2^{-\ell})\). Iteratively choosing a constant number of such primes at level \(\ell\) (each time ensuring we minimize _Z(p_)) decreases \(\Phi^{(\ell)}\) by the desired \(2^{7\ell}\) factor.

Given the above hierarchy, we proceed to search blocks in a depth-first order. For any given pair (_i,j_), iterate over all level 0 blocks. At each block, we will check whether it is a candidate block (as before with \[AV26\]), and if so process its children in depth-first order. At the final level of the hierarchy, we enumerate elements in all candidate blocks, and terminate the search for (_i,j_) whenever a true witness is found. The depth-first order of the traversal ensures that at level \(\ell\), at most 1 true block witness is examined. Thus, the total number of level \(\ell\) blocks examined at level \(\ell\) is at most \(O(N^2+\Phi^{(\ell-1)})\), since we must also examine the children of false level \(\ell-1\) candidates. Since \(\Phi^{(\ell)}\) is decreasing in \(\ell\), our algorithm makes progressively fewer queries to the matrix product computed by \[AV26\] at higher levels \(\ell\), but incurs higher preprocessing cost as the inner dimension \(D^{(\ell)}:=B^{(\ell)}P\) is decreasing in \(\ell\). Thus, instead of using Theorem 1.2, we use the data structure version of Theorem 25 (see Corollary 31 of \[AV26\]) which allows us to obtain faster preprocessing at the cost of slower queries.
